camel.origin: Camel hair in textiles is associated above all with the two-humped Bactrian camel, Camelus bactrianus, of the cold deserts of Central and East Asia, and fiber studies also cover the one-humped dromedary, C. dromedarius. Old World camels were domesticated roughly 3,000 to 6,000 years ago and still supply milk, meat, draught and wool; in Kazakhstan, for example, camels are raised as meat, dairy and wool animals. The wild two-humped camel, Camelus ferus, is a separate, critically endangered species whose lineage diverged from domestic Bactrians around a million years ago.
camel.structure: Camel coat is a double coat of keratin fibers: coarse, often medullated outer hair over a fine, soft undercoat. In a year-long follicle study of Iranian dromedaries, mean fiber diameter was about 19 microns, about 18% of fibers were medullated, clean yield was about 78%, and the ratio of secondary to primary follicles averaged about 6.9. In Sudanese camels, fiber diameter correlated strongly with prickle factor (r = 0.83) and with the share of medullated fibers (r = 0.73), so the coarse fraction drives discomfort. The natural tan to brown color comes from melanin pigment.
camel.process: The coat grows and sheds seasonally; in dromedaries, follicle activity fell to a minimum in February and recovered in spring. Loosened undercoat is gathered by hand, combed or shorn around the molt, then sorted by color and fineness and scoured. Dehairing, on machinery of the kind used for cashmere, removes coarse outer hair, which is used separately for coarser products. The dehaired undercoat is carded and spun on woollen or worsted systems, often left undyed to use its natural color or blended with wool for coating fabrics.
camel.performance: Dehaired camel undercoat is light, warm and soft, with the hygroscopic, self-extinguishing behavior of keratin and an affinity for acid dyes, though its natural color limits pale shades without bleaching. Because it is fine and often lightly twisted, it abrades and pills more readily than tightly spun worsted wool, and brushed coat surfaces flatten with wear. Residual coarse, medullated hair raises prickle. Like other animal fibers it is attacked by clothes moth and carpet beetle larvae and weakened by alkaline washing.
camel.identify: Burn tests (indicative only, and to be done with care) show keratin behavior. Microscopy of diameter, scale pattern and medullation is the usual first step, and because camel-colored cloth is common, a label claim should be checked by fiber analysis rather than color. MALDI-TOF peptide profiling and ATR-FTIR with chemometrics have both distinguished camel from cashmere, wool, mohair, yak, alpaca and other animal fibers. Hybrid camels bred from dromedary and Bactrian parents complicate species claims, and diagnostic SNP panels can detect hybrid ancestry in live animals.
camel.labeling: The US Wool Products Labeling Act of 1939 includes camel hair among the specialty fibers within the definition of wool, and FTC rules exclude it from the catch-all term fur fiber, so a product may state camel hair with its percentage. In the EU, Annex I of Regulation (EU) No 1007/2011 lists camel among the named fine animal hairs, followed or not by wool or hair. The color word camel is not a fiber name: a camel-colored coat made of wool or polyester must still carry its actual fiber content.
camel.past: Camels carried people and goods along cross-continental caravan routes and supplied wool as well as milk, meat and draught; archaeological dating places two-humped camel domestication about 5,000 to 6,000 years ago, and genetic work shows the living wild camel is a separate lineage rather than the direct ancestor of domestic Bactrians. Hybrids between dromedaries and Bactrians, once valued as strong pack animals, are now bred in the Middle East and Central Asia partly to improve milk or wool quality. Conservation geneticists stress keeping domestic herds diverse and protecting the last wild two-humped camels in Mongolia and China.

guanaco.origin: The guanaco, Lama guanicoe, is the largest wild artiodactyl of South America and the wild ancestor of the llama. Its range runs from the Peruvian Andes to Tierra del Fuego, with a northwestern subspecies, L. g. cacsilensis, and a southeastern one, L. g. guanicoe. Numbers are very uneven: distance sampling estimated about 1.1 million in Santa Cruz province alone, and more than two million persist in continental Patagonia, whereas only relict groups remain in the Gran Chaco and the Peruvian government classifies its local population as critically endangered.
guanaco.structure: Guanaco fleece is double-coated, with a fine, soft undercoat and coarser guard hair, both alpha-keratin fibers with a scaled cuticle and variable medullation; the undercoat is the textile fraction. Published diameter values differ with population and method, so no single figure is given here, and buyers should rely on laboratory measurement of the lot. Chemically, guanaco fleece carries a lipid profile of fatty acids, cholesterol and related compounds that mass spectrometry distinguishes from both vicuna and alpaca, even though infrared spectra could not separate guanaco from vicuna.
guanaco.process: Commercial fiber comes from capture and shearing of wild or semi-captive guanacos; in Argentine Patagonia, animals captured in the wild have been kept in semi-captivity for fiber production. Animals are gathered, restrained, shorn and released, and hormone studies show measurable stress responses to handling, shearing and release, one reason handling protocols matter. The fleece is then skirted, scoured and dehaired to remove guard hair before carding and spinning.
guanaco.performance: Dehaired guanaco down shares the hygroscopic, self-extinguishing and acid-dyeable behavior of other keratin fibers and gives light, warm, soft fabrics. Its fineness makes it vulnerable to abrasion and pilling in lightly twisted knits and scarves, and any guard hair left after dehairing is felt as prickle and seen as coarse, straight fibers on the surface. It must be protected from clothes moth and carpet beetle larvae and from harsh alkaline washing.
guanaco.identify: Burn tests (indicative only, and to be done with care) show keratin behavior. Hair morphology does not reliably separate camelid species, and in a forensic study infrared spectroscopy distinguished alpaca but not guanaco from vicuna, whereas direct-analysis-in-real-time mass spectrometry separated all three with high cross-validated accuracy. DNA methods combining mitochondrial cytochrome b, microsatellites and the SRY sex marker have identified poached guanaco in Chilean Patagonia, and similar tools could support provenance checks on raw fiber.
guanaco.labeling: Guanaco is not named in the US Wool Products Labeling Act, so its content is disclosed under 16 CFR 303.6, using the animal's name with hair, fiber or blend, for example guanaco hair, when present at 5% or more, or the collective term fur fiber. In the EU, Annex I of Regulation (EU) No 1007/2011 lists guanaco among the named fine animal hairs, followed or not by wool or hair. Because guanaco is a wild species, buyers should also check current CITES requirements and national permits for the specific lot.
guanaco.past: Guanaco populations were reduced and displaced by hunting and by sheep ranching, which brought fences and overgrazing to the Patagonian steppe; a 36-year series from Tierra del Fuego found that sheep density strongly depressed guanaco population growth. Where sheep numbers fell, guanacos rebounded and genetically separated groups reconnected. This recovery prompted proposals for sustainable use of guanacos on degraded land that no longer supports profitable sheep, alongside conflicts with farmers in southern Peru, where hunting the critically endangered local population is illegal. Guanacos were also introduced to Staats Island in the Falklands in the 1930s.
